title: Jacob goes down to Egypt (Genesis 46:1–7)
hookLine: the old man hears: fear not, I will go down with you

cards: The brothers ride home with Egyptian wagons and tell their father the impossible: Joseph is alive, and governor over all the land of Egypt. The old man's heart goes numb, the text says. He doesn't believe them.
Then he sees the wagons Joseph sent to carry him, and something in him wakes up. "It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive: I will go and see him before I die." But going means leaving.
Jacob is old; soon he'll tell Pharaoh he is a hundred and thirty. He'd be moving his whole family to a foreign country, in a famine, at the end of his life.

teach.b: Jacob sets out, and stops at Beersheba, on the southern edge of the land. His grandfather Abraham planted a tree there. His father Isaac built an altar there.
And there's a reason to stop and ask.

teach.h: ISAAC WAS TOLD: DON'T GO DOWN.
teach.b: Years before, in a famine, God had told Isaac: don't go down to Egypt. Now Jacob is about to do it.
So he offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac, and that night God speaks in a vision, in the King James Bible: "Jacob, Jacob. And he said, Here am I."
The same answer Abraham gave on the mountain, and Moses will give at the bush.
Then: "fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation: I will go down with thee into Egypt; and I will also surely bring thee up again."
It doesn't say this will be easy, or even that he'll come home alive. It says, I'm coming with you, and I'll bring you up again. Jacob will die in Egypt, and his body will be carried home.
The great nation will come up out of Egypt generations later, through a sea. Then a tender promise: Joseph shall put his hand upon your eyes. You'll die with your son beside you.
So seventy souls go down, the text counts, with their flocks and children.

teach.h: I WILL GO DOWN WITH THEE INTO EGYPT.
teach.b: Some Christians hear that promise again in the last line of Matthew's Gospel, where the risen Jesus says he is with his followers always.

how: Some Christians turn to God's words to Jacob, "I will go down with thee," when moving, emigrating or facing the end of life, and hear them alongside Jesus's promise in Matthew 28:20 to be with his followers always.

o: here am I, an answer when God calls
a blessing a father gives his sons
a prayer asking God for safe travel

games.q: what's inside the journey — tap the pairs.
p: where Jacob stopped to offer sacrifice

s: at first Jacob didn't believe Joseph was alive
his heart went numb; then he saw the wagons.
God promised Jacob he would return home alive
God promised to go down with him and bring him up again. Jacob dies in Egypt and is carried home.
Isaac had once been told not to go down to Egypt
in an earlier famine, Genesis 26 says. it's why Jacob stops to ask.

games.q: you're Jacob, an old man. your lost son is alive in Egypt, but your father was once told never to go there. you've reached the edge of the land. what do you do?
o: turn back; it's too big a risk at your age.
stop at Beersheba and offer sacrifice to the God of your father.
send the family ahead and stay behind alone.
games.why: he stops at Beersheba and sacrifices, and that night God says: fear not, I will go down with thee into Egypt.

practice: Name a move you're afraid of: a new city, a parent coming to live with you, or an inner one, like a new stage of life or letting go of something you know.
Notice where the fear sits in your body, then picture someone going with you. If you pray, you can bring this move to God; if you don't, picture the person you'd most want beside you.

wordCard.voice: Hineni. Hebrew for here am I: Jacob's answer to God in the night, before going down to Egypt with the promise, I will go down with thee.

orig.note: Hebrew: here am I. Abraham, Jacob and later Moses all answer God with this one word.

carryVoice: Your line: I will go with you. Jacob didn't go down alone. See you tomorrow.
